label: Yellowing older (lower) leaves
causes: Nitrogen deficiency - the plant moves nitrogen from old leaves to new growth
Natural aging if it's just one or two bottom leaves
Overwatering suffocating the roots
action: If many lower leaves yellow at once, feed with a balanced or nitrogen-leaning fertilizer and check that the pot drains. One old leaf now and then is normal.

label: Yellow new leaves with green veins
causes: Iron or manganese deficiency, usually caused by soil pH being too high (not actual lack of iron)
Very common in citrus, gardenia, blueberry and other acid-lovers
Constantly soggy soil blocking micronutrient uptake
action: Use an acid-formula fertilizer or chelated iron, and water acid-loving plants with rainwater instead of hard tap water. Fix drainage if soil stays wet.

label: Older leaves yellow between veins
causes: Magnesium deficiency - classic on tomatoes, citrus and roses
Potassium deficiency if edges scorch too
action: Water in Epsom salt (1 tablespoon per 4 liters) for magnesium, or switch to a feed with magnesium listed. Recheck in 2-3 weeks on new growth.

label: Brown, crispy leaf tips or edges
causes: Fertilizer salt buildup in the pot
Low humidity or underwatering
Fluoride/chlorine in tap water (dracaena, spider plant, calathea are sensitive)
action: Flush the pot with plenty of plain water, cut feeding in half, and for sensitive houseplants use rainwater, distilled or overnight-rested water.

label: Purple or reddish tint on leaves
causes: Phosphorus deficiency, especially in cold soil early in the season
Normal coloring in some varieties and in cool weather
action: If it's spring and soil is cold, wait - it often fixes itself as soil warms. Otherwise apply a phosphorus-containing feed (bone meal or bloom formula).

label: Brown/black spots on leaves
causes: Fungal leaf spot (often round spots, sometimes with yellow halo)
Bacterial spot (water-soaked, angular spots between veins)
Sunburn if spots are bleached and only on the most exposed leaves
action: Remove the worst leaves, stop wetting the foliage, water at the base in the morning, and improve airflow. Copper spray slows both fungal and bacterial spots.

label: White powdery coating on leaves
causes: Powdery mildew - thrives in warm days, cool nights and still air
Very common on squash, cucumbers, roses, phlox and bee balm
action: Remove the worst leaves, improve air circulation, and spray with potassium bicarbonate or sulfur. Unlike most fungi, it loves dry leaves - rinsing foliage actually helps.

label: Gray fuzzy mold on leaves, stems or flowers
causes: Botrytis (gray mold) - strikes in cool, damp, crowded conditions
Dead flowers and debris left on the plant feeding the fungus
action: Remove all affected parts and dead material, space plants out, and ventilate. Keep water off flowers and leaves.

label: Wilting even though soil is moist
causes: Root rot from overwatering - damaged roots can't drink, so the plant wilts in wet soil
Soil fungal wilts (verticillium, fusarium) in tomatoes and relatives
action: Stop watering, let the soil dry, and check roots: healthy ones are white and firm, rotten ones brown and mushy. Repot into fresh, fast-draining mix after trimming rot.

label: Wilting with dry soil
causes: Simple underwatering
Pot-bound roots or hydrophobic potting mix that sheds water
action: Water deeply until it runs from the drain holes; for shrunken peat mix, soak the whole pot in a basin for 20 minutes. Repot if roots circle the pot.

label: Leggy, stretched, pale growth
causes: Not enough light - the plant is reaching for it
Too much nitrogen combined with low light
action: Move it to brighter light (gradually, to avoid sunburn) and ease off feeding until growth is compact again. Fertilizer cannot substitute for light.

label: No flowers, or buds drop before opening
causes: Too much nitrogen (lush leaves, no blooms)
Not enough light
Temperature or watering swings during bud set (classic in gardenia, hibiscus, citrus)
action: Switch to a low-nitrogen, higher phosphorus-potassium feed, give more light, and keep water and temperature steady while buds form.

label: Sticky residue, tiny insects, or fine webbing
causes: Aphids, scale or whitefly (sticky honeydew on leaves and surfaces below)
Spider mites if there's fine webbing and stippled, dusty-looking leaves
action: Wash the plant with a strong water spray (undersides too), then treat weekly with insecticidal soap or horticultural oil until clear. Isolate houseplants from the others.

label: Holes or chewed leaf edges
causes: Caterpillars (ragged holes, droppings under leaves)
Slugs and snails (irregular holes plus slime trails, damage overnight)
Flea beetles (many tiny shot-holes)
action: Hand-pick caterpillars and check leaf undersides for eggs; use beer traps or barriers for slugs; row cover protects young plants from beetles.

label: Dark sunken patch on fruit bottom (tomato/pepper)
causes: Calcium not reaching the fruit - almost always caused by uneven watering, not missing calcium
Excess nitrogen making leafy growth outcompete fruit for calcium
action: Water deeply and consistently (mulch helps a lot), ease off high-nitrogen feeds. Affected fruit won't recover, but the next ones will be fine.

label: Barely growing / stunted overall
causes: General nutrient hunger in exhausted soil
Root-bound pot or compacted soil
Cold: most plants pause below ~10 °C, houseplants in winter
action: If it's the growing season and roots have room, feed with a balanced fertilizer and refresh the top layer with compost. Repot root-bound plants one size up.
